scenes.vo: Nine a.m. Another vendor to onboard. Here we go.
Inbox. Spreadsheet. Vendor call. Licences. A competitor price drop. All before lunch.
One vendor. About eighteen hours, by my research estimate.

Here's a live vendor call. The agent transcribes it and fills the gap table as the vendor talks. Fifteen percent base, plus twenty percent marketing support if I sell two thousand units in ninety days. Sounds like thirty-five. But Python simulates the demand: the chance of hitting two thousand is under a tenth of a percent. Reject the structure. And it hands me my next line: a target of 250 units, which we hit sixty percent of the time, or twenty-two percent guaranteed.

Every number the agent states cites its source, and Python re-checks it. In the live run, the model read this GST certificate twice: once as first of April 2023, once as 2025. The verifier won't pick a side; it flags it for me. And on our test set of 200 planted errors, it caught 198, with zero false alarms.

Vendors send scans, not data. The model reads the licence: valid until thirtieth November, though the application said twenty twenty-seven. SAM cuts out the label panel, it's read again, and the label says thirty percent protein where the sheet claims thirty-two. The price list says three thousand three fifty-two where the sheet says three thousand three twenty-five. Caught before listing, not after a complaint.

Then it runs the category. Price requests. Catalog fixes: thirty-six issues, thirty-two fixed. Promotions, and price watch. Every rule lives in one playbook I can edit. And it works for pet, beauty, electronics, or your own upload.
Across a category team, that's about a third of the week back. Modelled, not yet measured.
Five Meta models, each doing something code can't. I'm Meera, and this is CategoryOS. Try it yourself.
